analysis.one_liner: Repeals the federal estate tax while locking in the gift tax exemption.
analysis.headline: The estate tax repeal bill drew 102 House cosponsors, but the Ways and Means Committee never held a markup and the full House never voted on it.
analysis.plain_summary: This bill would eliminate the federal estate tax and the generation-skipping transfer tax for people dying after enactment. It would also make the gift tax's maximum 35% rate and its lifetime exemption (starting at $5 million) permanent, with the exemption adjusted for inflation. Only the very largest estates ever owe the estate tax, so the bill's benefits would flow almost entirely to the heirs of the wealthiest households, while the lost revenue would have to be made up by other taxpayers or borrowing.
analysis.who_benefits: Heirs of very large estates. The estate tax only applies to estates above roughly $5.5 million per person (about $11 million per married couple), so only a few thousand estates a year pay it, and they are overwhelmingly the wealthiest households. Wealth owners who plan to pass on millions would save up to 40% of everything above the exemption.

how_it_helps.text: Repeals the estate tax for the estates of anyone dying on or after the bill's enactment.
Repeals the generation-skipping transfer tax, which taxes very large transfers that skip a generation, such as money left directly to grandchildren.
Makes the gift tax's maximum 35% rate permanent and locks in a $5 million lifetime gift tax exemption, adjusted for inflation.

analysis.who_pays: The federal treasury, and ultimately everyone else who pays taxes. Revenue that the estate tax brings in from a few thousand very large estates each year would disappear, so the burden would shift to other taxpayers or to future generations through borrowing. Heirs would also keep unrealized investment gains untouched, since the bill makes no change to the rule that resets an inherited asset's value for tax purposes at death.

drawbacks.text: Repealing the estate and generation-skipping transfer taxes eliminates a revenue stream that currently comes only from the largest estates, shifting the federal tax burden onto everyone else.

The bill keeps the gift tax but makes its $5 million lifetime exemption permanent, so a wealthy person could give away up to $5 million during life tax-free and pass the rest at death untaxed — the richest households get both ends of the loophole.

Because the bill leaves the inherited-asset basis rule unchanged, unrealized investment gains would escape both income tax and estate tax entirely, a break available only to families wealthy enough to own significant appreciated assets.

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: The benefits go almost entirely to a few thousand very wealthy families a year, while the cost — lost federal revenue — is spread across all taxpayers. Supporters argue repeal protects family farms and small businesses, but only estates above roughly $11 million per couple owe the tax at all, and the bill retains a large tax-free lifetime gift exemption that mainly serves the same households. The costs outweigh the benefits for the general public.

outcome.mechanism: It was referred to the House Ways and Means Committee the day it was introduced, and the committee never brought it up — no hearing, no markup, no floor vote before Congress ended.

narrative.text: The bill was introduced on January 24, 2017, by Rep. Kristi Noem with six original cosponsors.
It gathered 102 cosponsors in total — 101 Republicans and 1 Democrat.
The bill was referred to the House Committee on Ways and Means on the day of introduction, and no further action was ever taken on it.

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: Ordinary federal taxpayers came out ahead: the estate tax stayed in place, so revenue continues to come from the largest estates rather than from everyone else. The wealthy families and their congressional supporters lost their push for full repeal, though Congress later addressed the estate tax in the 2017 tax law by doubling the exemption instead of repealing it.

analysis.who_came_out_ahead_short: Federal taxpayers who keep the estate tax

for.name: Rep. Kristi Noem
for.what_they_did: Introduced the bill and recruited cosponsors.

for.name: Rep. Rob Bishop of Georgia, Rep. Devin Nunes, Rep. Adrian Smith of Nebraska and three other original cosponsors
for.what_they_did: Joined the bill as original cosponsors on the day of introduction.

against.name: Rep. Kevin Brady
against.role: Chair, House Ways and Means Committee
against.what_they_did: As chairman of the committee the bill was referred to, never scheduled a hearing or markup on it, so it never advanced.

against.name: House Republican leadership
against.role: Speaker and majority leadership of the House
against.what_they_did: Never brought the standalone repeal bill to the House floor; the estate tax was later partially addressed in the 2017 tax bill by doubling the exemption instead.

sides.party_line_note: 101 of the bill's 102 cosponsors were Republicans; a single Democrat signed on, and the bill sat in committee under a Republican majority.

industries.note: Repeal would have saved estates above roughly $11 million per couple up to 40% of their value, a benefit concentrated in a few thousand families a year. The revenue loss would fall on everyone else through other taxes or borrowing.

industries.industry: Estate planning attorneys and wealth advisors
industries.note: Full repeal would shrink the market for estate-tax planning services that exists only because the tax exists. Their loss runs in the same direction as the public's interest in keeping the tax, though the public's interest is about revenue rather than their fees.
